title: Squarefree Sumset
content:
**SquarefreeSumset A** requires that $a + b$ is squarefree for ALL $a, b \in A$ (including $a = b$, so $2a$ must also be squarefree).

**Lean**: `∀ a ∈ A, ∀ b ∈ A, Squarefree (a + b)`

**Why this is restrictive**: A number $n$ is squarefree iff no prime square $p^2$ divides $n$. For each prime $p$, the condition $p^2 \nmid (a + b)$ eliminates roughly a $1/p^2$ fraction of pairs. Requiring this for ALL primes simultaneously is extremely constraining — the set $A$ must avoid a complicated pattern of residue classes modulo $p^2$ for every prime $p$.

**Density perspective**: Squarefree numbers have density $6/\pi^2 \approx 0.608$, but the sumset condition is much stronger than just requiring elements to be squarefree.

title: Set Enumeration
content:
**enumSet A j** is the $j$-th smallest element of $A$, axiomatized as a strictly monotone function with $\text{range}(\text{enumSet } A) = A$.

**Why axiomatize**: Constructing the $j$-th element of an infinite set in Lean requires well-ordering machinery. Since we only need the *existence* of such an enumeration (which follows from the well-ordering of $\mathbb{N}$), axiomatization is cleaner. The `enumSet_spec` axiom guarantees both `StrictMono (enumSet A)` and surjectivity onto $A$.

**Growth rate language**: The conjecture asks about the growth rate of $a_j = \text{enumSet } A \; j$ as $j \to \infty$. StrictMono ensures $a_j < a_{j+1}$, so the sequence is a valid increasing enumeration.
mathContext: enumSet A j = j-th element of A (strictly monotone, range = A)

title: Exponential Growth Conjecture
content:
**ErdosProblem1103**: Every infinite squarefree-sumset sequence grows at least exponentially.

**Formal statement**: $\forall A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, if $A$ is infinite and $\text{SquarefreeSumset}(A)$, then $\exists C > 1$ such that $C^j \leq a_j$ for all sufficiently large $j$.

**Lean**: Uses `∀ᶠ j in atTop` (Mathlib's Filter.atTop) for the 'eventually for large $j$' quantifier, and `C ^ (j : ℝ)` for real-valued exponential comparison.

**Status**: OPEN. The best known lower bound is polynomial ($j^{4/3}$), far from exponential. The best known upper bound is subexponential ($\exp(5j/\log j)$), which is slower than any $C^j$ for $C > 1$.

title: van Doorn–Tao Upper Bound
content:
**Van Doorn–Tao (2025)**: There EXISTS an infinite squarefree-sumset sequence with subexponential growth:

$$a_j < \exp\left(\frac{5j}{\log j}\right) \quad \text{for large } j$$

This is subexponential because $5j/\log j = o(j)$, so $\exp(5j/\log j) = o(C^j)$ for any $C > 1$.

**Significance**: If the conjecture (exponential growth is necessary) is TRUE, then this construction must fail to satisfy the squarefree-sumset condition. If the conjecture is FALSE, constructions like this — or even slower-growing ones — might work.

**Axiomatized** because the construction involves deep analytic number theory.

title: van Doorn–Tao Lower Bound
content:
**Van Doorn–Tao (2025)**: ANY infinite squarefree-sumset sequence satisfies:

$$a_j > 0.24 \cdot j^{4/3} \quad \text{for all } j$$

The exponent $4/3$ means the sequence must grow at least as fast as $j^{4/3}$, which is faster than linear but far slower than exponential.

**Gap**: The lower bound is polynomial ($j^{4/3}$) while the upper bound is subexponential ($\exp(5j/\log j)$). Closing this gap — or showing that the true threshold is exponential — is the core of Problem 1103.

**Axiomatized** because the proof uses sieve methods and analytic techniques.

title: Konyagin Finite Bound
content:
**Konyagin**: For a FINITE set $A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ with squarefree sumset:

$$|A| \leq C \cdot N^{11/15}$$

The exponent $11/15 \approx 0.733$ means the set $A$ can contain at most about $N^{0.733}$ elements out of $\{1, \ldots, N\}$. This is a density-type result: as $N \to \infty$, the proportion $|A|/N \to 0$.

**Lean**: Formalized with Finset (finite sets), explicit constant $C > 0$, and conditions $\forall a \in A, a \leq N$ and squarefree pairwise sums.

**Connection to infinite case**: The finite bound implies that squarefree-sumset sequences must be sparse, but doesn't directly give the infinite-sequence growth rate.
